chapters.title: Hook and promise
chapters.text: Have you ever wondered how to make technology work for you instead of spending hours figuring everything out? Welcome to episode 28 of AI for Beginners. Today, we’re looking at ai music and sound effects. By the end, you’ll understand one practical idea, watch a realistic example, and try a small exercise yourself. You don’t need a technical background or expensive software. Bring your curiosity. We’ll work through it together. Here’s the example we’ll use: a subtle electronic intro sound. We’ll use that situation to make the topic concrete. Watch how we break the task into small steps, because the same thinking will help you use many different AI tools later in this course.

chapters.title: Explain the concept
chapters.text:
Let’s start with the main idea. choose appropriate background audio for educational videos.

Think of AI as a tool that processes information and returns an output based on its training, instructions, and any relevant information it can access. It can save time on drafts and patterns, but it doesn’t automatically know what’s correct for your situation. The most useful habit is to define what you want before touching the tool.

Ask yourself three questions: what’s my goal, what information does the tool need, and how will I check the result? Those questions work whether you’re writing a prompt, building a workflow, or reviewing a generated answer.

chapters.title: On-screen demonstration
chapters.text:
Let’s try it with an example. Our example is a subtle electronic intro sound.

Start by writing down the desired result in one sentence. Next, identify the input: what would a person need to know to do this task correctly? Then write a simple instruction with that context and a clear format. On screen, I am showing a sample request, followed by a possible output. Notice that we’re not judging the result by how impressive it sounds. We’re checking whether it actually meets the task. If the output is too broad, ask for a more specific version. If a fact matters, verify it from a reliable source.

chapters.title: Guided beginner exercise
chapters.text: Your turn. Try this exercise: build an audio cue sheet. Begin with a very small example, not a complex project. Give yourself thirty seconds to decide what success would look like. Then complete the task once and inspect the result. What’s useful? What’s missing? What would you change? Make one improvement and compare the first and second versions. This simple before-and-after comparison teaches you more than copying a complicated prompt from the internet. If your chosen tool is unavailable, do the exercise on paper: sketch the input, the steps, and the output. The objective is to practice the underlying thinking, not to depend on one particular app.
